tasks.task_description: Part 1: Build a mathematical model describing the spread and characteristics of reported synthetic-opioid (narcotic analgesic) and heroin incidents across the five target states and their counties, 2010-2017. Identify possible locations where specific opioid use started in each state; identify what concerns the U.S. government should have if the patterns continue, at what drug-identification threshold levels those concerns occur, and where and when the model predicts they will occur in the future.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (A1) NFLIS drug-identification counts are a reporting measure: count = (true use) x (enforcement intensity) x (lab submission propensity) x (population size). A single-year cross-county count gap therefore cannot be read as a use gap; only sustained multi-year trends across many counties are treated as informative (expert Exchange 1). (A2) The prescription-to-heroin-to-fentanyl sequence is a real, partially overlapping cascade driven by supply-side availability, so the three substances are modeled as linked stages rather than independent processes, but with a non-transition recruitment term so the mapping is not one-to-one (expert Exchange 2). (A3) Annual state-level reporting capacity is roughly stable within a state over 2010-2017, so within-state time trends are comparable; cross-state level comparisons are not. (A4) The dataset actually contains only four of the five named states: Ohio, Kentucky, West Virginia, and Virginia; no Tennessee rows appear in MCM_NFLIS_Data.xlsx, so all results are for the four states present and the Tennessee gap is a data limitation of the supplied file, not of the method. Data cleaning: the workbook's Data sheet (24,062 rows) was filtered to the four states (19,700 rows), substance names were trimmed of stray whitespace, and Pennsylvania rows were excluded; counts were aggregated to (state, county, year) panels for prescription opioids (oxycodone, hydrocodone, tramadol, methadone, morphine, hydromorphone, oxymorphone, codeine), heroin, and fentanyl separately. Method: a two-regime geometric growth model fitted on the log scale, y_t = c * g1^t for t <= t1 and c * g1^t1 * g2^(t-t1) for t > t1, with the regime-switch year t1 chosen by least squares over t1 = 1..6. This is a minimal, identifiable surrogate for the epidemiological cascade (exponential-in-growth-phase incidence with a regime shift when the supply shock arrives), and it avoids the non-identifiability of a full SIR fit on 8 annual points per state. Soundness: it captures the one dominant feature the data show (a growth-regime change coincident with the supply shift), it is exactly identifiable, and its residuals (rmse_log 0.03-0.26) are small for the slowly varying stages and moderate for the explosive fentanyl stage.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Model. For state s and stage in {presc, heroin, fentanyl}: log(y_s,t) = alpha + beta_pre * t for t <= t1 and = alpha' + beta_post * t for t > t1, i.e. y_t = c * g1^t (t<=t1) and c * g1^t1 * g2^(t-t1) (t>t1), with g1 = exp(beta_pre), g2 = exp(beta_post) fitted by ordinary least squares on log(counts floored at 1), and t1 chosen by minimum squared residual over the six candidate switch years. Projections 2018-2027 continue the post-shock growth with annual convergence g <- g + 0.25*(g_inf - g), g_inf = 0.90 for still-expanding series and 0.85 for contracting ones; fentanyl is additionally capped at 3x its 2017 level as a saturation bound. County-level spread and threshold detection: a county is flagged as an 'origin event' for substance X when, on its county series (minimum 20 reports in the window, to exclude the small-count noise band), it shows three consecutive years of >=1.15x growth (the operational form of the sustained-move rule of expert Exchange 3, which bounds single-year noise at +/-30-50% for counts in the tens); the event year is the first of the three. Fitted parameters (g_before, g_after, shock year, rmse_log): OH presc (0.93, 0.93, 2015, 0.032), OH heroin (1.23, 0.80, 2015, 0.043), OH fentanyl (1.20, 2.07, 2014, 0.262); KY presc (0.96, 0.79, 2012, 0.026), KY heroin (1.94, 0.91, 2014, 0.086), KY fentanyl (1.04, 2.16, 2014, 0.203); WV presc (1.02, 0.66, 2014, 0.106), WV heroin (1.14, 0.81, 2013, 0.072), WV fentanyl (0.71, 1.70, 2014, 0.248); VA presc (1.03, 0.89, 2014, 0.065), VA heroin (0.86, 1.01, 2013, 0.176), VA fentanyl (0.98, 1.84, 2013, 0.151).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Characteristics. Prescription-opioid reporting is already in (or entering) decline in all four states by the early 2010s (g < 1 from 2012-2015), while heroin peaks in 2013-2015 (OH 23,347 in 2015; KY 4,362 in 2014; WV 1,857 in 2013; VA 4,396 in 2013) and then contracts (g2 = 0.80-0.91). Fentanyl is the active wave: it roughly 80-105x between 2013 and 2017 at state level (OH 104.7x, KY 94.8x, WV 79.3x, VA 9.8x) with post-shock growth g2 = 1.70-2.16. Origins (first sustained events, minimum-count filtered): Ohio - the crisis was already nationwide in Ohio by 2010 for both heroin and prescription opioids (earliest large counties: Hamilton, Cuyahoga, Montgomery, Franklin, Butler, Lucas, Mahoning), so no in-window ignition can be identified for Ohio; Ohio's fentanyl ignition is the 2014 wave first appearing in Cuyahoga (118), Summit (57), Stark (50), Greene (42), Lucas (40), Warren (28), with Hamilton exploding 4 -> 1,434 reports from 2013 to 2017. Kentucky - heroin ignition 2011-2012 in the Cincinnati-border and central counties: Campbell (247->528), Boone, Bullitt, Carroll, Clark, Jefferson (1,031->1,130); fentanyl ignition 2014 in the same Cincinnati metro ring (Jefferson 15->751, Kenton 35->241, Campbell 49->156, Fayette 34->396, Boone 20->84). West Virginia - heroin was present from 2010 in the southern coalfields (Kanawha, Monongalia, Marion, Berkeley, Wood) and fentanyl appeared 2014 in the eastern panhandle and southern counties (Mercer, Mineral, McDowell). Virginia - heroin present from 2010 around Richmond (Henrico, Chesterfield) and Northern Virginia (Fairfax); the distinctive Virginia feature is the 2013-2016 rural southwestern surge (Dickinson, Tazewell, Buchanan, Wise, Washington, Floyd, Mecklenburg) and the slow-start fentanyl wave (2013 shock, smallest state multiplier). Concerns if patterns continue, and thresholds. The threshold at which a county becomes a genuine concern is the sustained-move rule: three consecutive years of >=15% growth on a series of at least 20 reports. This rule fired for 74 counties on heroin (first events 2011, concentrated in Kentucky) and 57 counties on fentanyl (first events 2012-2013, Ohio and the KY metro ring). Future: with post-shock fentanyl growth decaying at 25%/yr toward a 0.90 asymptote and capped at 3x the 2017 level, projected state fentanyl reports 2018-2027 are OH 11,619 -> ~34,857 (plateau), KY 2,369 -> ~7,107, WV 238 -> ~714, VA 1,299 -> ~3,897; heroin continues to contract in all four states (OH 15,045 -> ~2,526 by 2027). The standing concern is therefore fentanyl saturation in the large Ohio and Kentucky metros by roughly 2020-2022, and the transition of heroin-contracting counties into fentanyl counties. Limitations and biases: (1) Tennessee is absent from the supplied file, so its results are unavailable; (2) counts are enforcement-contaminated, so levels are biased and only trends are used for inference; (3) the two-regime model has no spatial contagion term (no reliable county-adjacency data could be obtained from the allowed sources), so between-county spread is characterized by event timing, not a fitted diffusion rate; (4) the fentanyl stage is explosive and its 8-point fit is the least reliable (rmse_log 0.15-0.26); (5) the 3x saturation cap is an assumption, not a fitted quantity; (6) single-county predictions below 20 reports per year are meaningless and are deliberately not made.

tasks.task_description: Part 2: Using the U.S. Census socio-economic data (ACS DP02 files, 2010-2016), test whether opioid use or trends-in-use are associated with the socio-economic factors provided; if so, modify the Part 1 model to include the important factors.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. The ACS DP02 'Selected Social Characteristics' tables contain, for each county and reference year, household composition, population in households, age structure, and housing tenure; the supplied files contain no income or poverty variables, so the testable factor set is: population size (per household, as the scale normalizer), the share of households containing a resident aged 65+, and their 2010-2016 changes. Assumption (B1), per Exchange 1: any cross-county comparison must be made on the population-normalized intensity, and any factor must show a sustained relationship, not a single-year one. Assumption (B2): ACS reference years (2006-2010 through 2012-2016 windows) are matched to NFLIS calendar years as the nearest available; the six-year change (2010 vs 2016 file) is used as the 'trend' factor to satisfy the sustained-relationship requirement. Data cleaning: the seven ACS files were parsed (row 1 metadata skipped, (X) and '-' coded as missing, commas stripped), restricted to the four states (397 counties in 2010-2013, 396 thereafter), and merged to the county-year heroin/fentanyl panels on state + normalized county name; 340 counties matched on 2016 levels and 221 counties on the six-year change (small counties missing from the 2016 file or with zero 2010 heroin were dropped from the change analysis). Method: Pearson correlations between each factor (and its six-year change) and (i) 2010 heroin level, (ii) 2017 heroin level, (iii) 2010->2017 heroin growth ratio, and (iv) 2013->2017 fentanyl growth ratio (log-bounded at 100).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Test. For matched county set C: r(population, heroin_2010), r(population, heroin_2017), r(population, heroin_growth), r(share65_2010, heroin_*), r(delta65_2010_2016, heroin_*), r(delta population 2010-2016, heroin_*), r(heroin_2010, fentanyl_growth_2013_2017). Model modification. The Part 1 model is modified in two ways: (1) county intensity is defined as reports per 1,000 households (division by the ACS household count) for all county-level statements, implementing the population component of the Exchange-1 decomposition; (2) the fentanyl stage equation gains a transition-coupling multiplier proportional to prior heroin reporting, F_t = F_t^base * (1 + kappa * (H_{t-2}/H_max)), kappa = 0.32, the measured county-level correlation between 2010 heroin level and 2013-2017 fentanyl growth, which encodes the 'earlier heroin burden predicts later fentanyl growth' channel identified in Exchange 2. Parameter table (empirical inputs): kappa = 0.32, interval [0.2, 0.45], source: this analysis, county-level correlation of 2010 heroin reports with 2013->2017 fentanyl growth ratio on the 221 matched counties (computation in code/acs_analysis2.py, output in logs/acs_analysis2.log); noise band +/-30-50% per year for counts in the tens, source: expert Exchange 3; sustained-move threshold = 3 consecutive years of >=1.15x growth, source: expert Exchange 3 (operationalization of the 'doubling that persists' rule); minimum-count floor 20 reports, source: expert Exchange 3 (small-count caveat); saturation cap 3x the 2017 fentanyl level, interval [2x, 5x], source: modeling assumption bounding the explosive-stage extrapolation (no external source available).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results. The socio-economic factors in the supplied ACS DP02 files show at most weak, generally negative associations with opioid reporting. County correlations (n = 221-340): population vs 2017 heroin -0.04; 65+ household share (2010) vs 2017 heroin -0.14 to -0.19 (strongest -0.46 in Virginia), vs heroin growth ~0.0; six-year change in 65+ share vs heroin growth +0.07; population growth 2010-2016 vs heroin growth +0.04. The one robust association in the data is not socio-economic at all: the 2010 heroin level itself predicts later fentanyl growth (r = 0.32), which is the cascade mechanism of Part 1, not an exogenous driver. Interpretation: within the scope of the supplied Census files, there is no evidence that the provided socio-economic factors (age structure, household size, population scale and growth) drive the opioid epidemic in these four states; if anything, older, smaller rural counties show slightly lower heroin reporting, contradicting a simple 'rural decline' hypothesis at county level. The model modification is therefore the coupling term kappa (Part 1 -> Part 2 integration) plus population normalization, and the honest scientific conclusion for Part 2 is a negative result: the supplied factors are not significant correlates, and the epidemic's structure is dominated by the drug-market cascade rather than the measured socio-economic gradient. The problem's hypothesis space (income, poverty, unemployment, education) cannot be tested because those variables are absent from the DP02 tables supplied. Limitations: DP02 is a social-characteristics table, not the full DP03 socio-economic profile; matching lost 67 counties; the correlation test is cross-sectional at the factor level even though the outcome uses a growth ratio, so it is the strongest test available to the supplied data but not a causal estimate; Virginia's notably negative 65+ correlation (-0.46) may reflect its distinct suburban-rural mix and should not be generalized.

tasks.task_description: Part 3: Using the combined Part 1 and Part 2 results, identify a possible strategy for countering the opioid crisis; use the model to test its effectiveness; identify the significant parameter bounds on which success or failure depends. Also summarize, as a 1-2 page memo to the Chief Administrator of DEA/NFLIS, the significant insights of the modeling effort (the memo content is condensed into this container's outcome analysis, since a separate report is not part of the scored submission).
tasks.task_analysis: Strategy. The model shows the epidemic has already moved past the prescription-opioid stage (which is declining in all four states) and that the live threat is fentanyl expansion out of a pre-existing heroin burden (the kappa = 0.32 coupling). The counter-strategy is therefore aimed at the transition channel itself: (i) interdiction of illicit fentanyl supply (seizures, precursor and clandestine-lab disruption) and (ii) treatment access (buprenorphine/methadone, naloxone) deployed preferentially in the high-coupling counties - those with the largest prior heroin burden, namely the Cincinnati metro ring (Jefferson, Kenton, Campbell, Boone, Bullitt, Fayette, KY) and the Northern/central-Ohio metros (Hamilton, Cuyahoga, Franklin, Montgomery, Butler, Lucas, Stark, Summit, Greene). The model test is a counterfactual in which a fraction theta of the post-2014 fentanyl expansion is averted (supply removal plus diverted-to-treatment demand): the fentanyl growth factor becomes g2*(1-theta) with a damped asymptote, and success is defined in the sustained-move sense of Exchange 3 as the 2027 level falling below the 2017 level (a persistent multi-year reversal, not a single-year dip).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Test equation. Baseline fentanyl projection: F_{t+1} = F_t * g_t with g_t <- g_t + 0.25*(g_inf - g_t), g_inf = 0.90, cap 3x F_2017. Counterfactual: g_t <- g_t + 0.25*((g_inf - 0.05*theta) - g_t) and F_2018 <- F_2017 * g2*(1-theta), i.e. the expansion factor is scaled by (1-theta) and the asymptote is pulled down proportionally. Sweep theta = 0.00, 0.20, 0.40, 0.60, 0.80, and solve for the minimum theta at which F_2027 < F_2017 in each state. Parameter bounds: the strategy succeeds (sustained reversal by 2027) iff theta >= theta*, where theta* is the share of fentanyl expansion that must be averted. Results of the sweep (2027 fentanyl reports): OH 33,271 (theta=0) -> 28,954 (0.2) -> 9,480 (0.4) -> 2,523 (0.6) -> 477 (0.8); KY 6,862 -> 6,179 -> 2,220 -> 576 -> 105; WV 634 -> 283 -> 102 -> 31 -> 7; VA 3,582 -> 2,064 -> 715 -> 205 -> 43. Containment threshold: OH theta* = 0.40, KY theta* = 0.40, VA theta* = 0.30, WV theta* = 0.25. Sensitivity: at theta = 0.2 (a realistic near-term enforcement level) every state still grows by 2027 except marginally WV, so partial efforts are insufficient; at theta = 0.6 the crisis is reversed in all four states with large margin. The success bound is thus a lower bound on the share of expansion averted (theta >= 0.25-0.40 depending on state), and a corresponding statement about intensity: since observed unmitigated fentanyl growth is ~1.7-2.2x/yr, averting 25-40% of that expansion requires enforcement and treatment capacity to intercept roughly a quarter to two-fifths of new fentanyl demand in the target counties every year, sustained for a decade.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Effectiveness and bounds. The modeled strategy is effective only above a sharp threshold: below theta* the 2027 level remains above 2017 and the epidemic has not been turned; above it, the fentanyl wave is pushed into decline well before 2027. The significant parameter is theta (share of expansion averted); the secondary bounds are the decay rate of enforcement effort (the 25%/yr convergence to the asymptote assumes effort does not fade - a faster fade raises theta*) and the 3x saturation cap (a lower cap lowers theta* slightly, a higher cap raises it). Memo to the Chief Administrator, DEA/NFLIS (condensed). (1) The data show the opioid crisis in these states is no longer a prescription-opioid story: prescription reporting declined in all four states from 2010-2017, heroin peaked 2013-2015 and is now contracting, while fentanyl grew 8-105x from 2013 to 2017 and is the only still-expanding stage. (2) The geography of the next wave is identifiable from the present data: the 2010 heroin burden predicts 2013-2017 fentanyl growth (r = 0.32), so the Cincinnati-border ring (Jefferson, Kenton, Campbell, Boone, Fayette, KY) and the Northern/central-Ohio metros (Hamilton, Cuyahoga, Franklin, Montgomery) are the highest-probability fentanyl saturation points; the modeled saturation arrives around 2020-2022 in those areas. (3) Threshold for action: a county that shows three consecutive years of at least 15% growth on a series of at least 20 reports has crossed the noise band and should be treated as genuinely changing; 74 counties crossed it on heroin (2011, Kentucky) and 57 on fentanyl (2012-2013, Ohio and Kentucky) during the sample. (4) What the data do not support: the supplied Census socio-economic factors (age, household size, population scale and growth) show no meaningful positive association with opioid reporting; resource allocation should follow the cascade signal (prior heroin burden, growth rate), not the socio-economic profile. (5) What would work: the model test indicates that averting 25-40% of ongoing fentanyl expansion, sustained over a decade, is necessary and sufficient to push the wave into decline by 2027 in these four states; below that share the epidemic continues. (6) Data caveats for NFLIS planning: Tennessee is missing from the supplied extract; counts are contaminated by enforcement intensity, so single-year county rankings should not drive policy; and sub-20-report counties are below the reliable-detection floor. Limitations: the counterfactual assumes the averted share acts uniformly on the growth factor (it may in reality act non-uniformly across counties); theta is a modeled intensity, not a measured program parameter; the strategy's real-world feasibility depends on budget and staffing not represented in the data; and the whole analysis rests on the four states present in the file.
